temptingClaims: The Michelson–Morley experiment is why Einstein wrote the paper.
whyTempting: Textbooks often begin special relativity with that experiment, and the paper does mention failed attempts to detect the earth's motion through the light medium.
whereItIsTrue: The paper counts the unsuccessful attempts to detect a motion of the earth relative to the light medium among the grounds for its conjecture (p. 891).

whatIsTrue.r0: The paper opens with a moving magnet and conductor, and beside them mentions unnamed, unsuccessful attempts to detect the earth's motion through the light medium. It names no experiment and no experimenter for them, and it says nothing of how Einstein came to the problem.
whatIsTrue.r1: The first paragraph describes a magnet and a conductor: the observable current depends only on their relative motion, while the usual view treats the two cases, magnet moving or conductor moving, quite differently (p. 891). The second adds: "examples of a similar kind, together with the unsuccessful attempts to detect a motion of the earth relative to the 'light medium'" lead to the conjecture that no properties of the phenomena correspond to absolute rest, and that the same laws hold in all the coordinate systems for which mechanics holds, "as has already been shown for the quantities of the first order" (p. 891). The conjecture is then raised to a postulate, beside the constancy of the velocity of light (pp. 891–892). The names Michelson and Morley appear nowhere in the paper. What led Einstein personally to the paper is a separate question from what the paper cites, and SR-02 sets out the asymmetry the paper actually opens with.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The paper's first example: a magnet and a conductor, with the same current whichever moves, but two different descriptions in the usual theory (p. 891). (2) Its second sentence of evidence: “Beispiele ähnlicher Art, sowie die mißlungenen Versuche, eine Bewegung der Erde relativ zum ‚Lichtmedium‘ zu konstatieren” (p. 891). (3) No experimenter, apparatus or result is named for those attempts, and the same sentence limits what had been shown to the quantities of the first order. (4) The conclusion drawn is a conjecture, raised to a postulate: the principle of relativity, with the constancy of the velocity of light added as a second (pp. 891–892). (5) So the paper's stated starting point is the asymmetry of description, with the failed attempts beside it, unnamed; neither Michelson nor Morley is named in any of its 31 pages.
whatIsTrue.r3: Einstein's later statements about which experiments he knew, and when, are evidence about his path to the paper, not about the paper's argument. They rest on later letters and recollections, which this record has not read and does not summarize.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 891–921 (1905), plates pp. 891–892
